pedagogy.summary: Children measure and calculate the perimeter of composite (rectilinear) shapes — figures with only straight sides and right angles, like an L-shape, that look like rectangles joined together. The distinctive skill is DEDUCING unmarked side lengths from the labelled ones (opposite sides of the whole must match, adding or subtracting known lengths) before totalling, and adding every boundary side exactly once. The main hazards are forgetting to find the missing sides and adding only the numbers given, mis-deducing a missing length, including internal split-lines, double-counting, and confusing perimeter with area.
bestPractices: Define a rectilinear/compound shape (straight sides, right angles; rectangles joined) and use both terms.
Deduce unmarked sides from labelled ones: the two shorter sides along a direction sum to the opposite longer side (add or subtract known lengths).
Mark each side as it is added so none is missed or counted twice, and check every side is included.
Distinguish the boundary (perimeter) from internal split-lines, which are not part of the perimeter.
Keep perimeter (length, cm) distinct from area (cm²).
keyRepresentations: L-shaped / rectilinear figure with some sides unmarked
commonMisconceptions: Forgets to find the unmarked sides and adds only the given numbers.
Cannot see that the two shorter sides equal the opposite longer side, so mis-deduces a missing length.
Includes internal lines, double-counts a side, or confuses perimeter with area.

learn.summary: Year 5 pupils measure and calculate the perimeter of composite rectilinear shapes (straight sides, with every corner made by sides meeting at right angles — rectangles joined, e.g. an L-shape). The distinctive skill is DEDUCING unmarked side lengths from the labelled ones: in each direction, the side lengths on one side of the shape add up to the side lengths on the opposite side. In an L-shape this means the two shorter sides along one direction add up to the opposite longer side (so a missing length is found by adding the two shorter sides, or by subtracting a known shorter side from the longer one); other shapes, such as U- or T-shapes, may have more than two parts on one side. Pupils then total every boundary side exactly once. Chief hazards: adding only the given numbers (forgetting missing sides), working out a missing length wrongly, including internal split-lines, double-counting a side, and confusing perimeter (a length in cm or m) with area (cm2 or m2).

activities.title: Trace-the-boundary L-shape with live missing-side reveal
feedback: If you reached an unmarked side and guessed, line it up against the opposite side(s) of the whole shape and add or subtract the known lengths — the total length across the shape in each direction must match.
If your total is too large, check whether you added an inside line or counted a side twice; a side should tick off only once as you trace.
If you added only the printed numbers, ask: have I found every unmarked side first? Mark each side before adding anything.
activities.rationale: Tracing the boundary while deducing unmarked sides is intended to make the deduction step — the crux of the topic — concrete, and ticking each side as it is added directly guards against the miscounting and double-counting the curriculum flags. An OPTIONAL interactive version can light and tick each side as the finger passes, keep the internal line greyed out, and pulse the two opposite labelled sides so their sum snaps onto the blank; these are illustrative mechanisms, not requirements, and the same work can be done on cm paper by hand.
sourceClaims: A rectilinear/compound shape has only straight sides and right angles (rectangles joined). Things to look out for: 'children may miscount when adding the sides of rectilinear shapes'; 'if children do not have a secure understanding of addition and subtraction, they may struggle when finding missing sides'; 'children may find it difficult to see that the two shorter sides are equal to the longer opposite side'. A reasoning task shows a character whose total wrongly 'includes sides that are inside the shape'. Children are 'encouraged to mark sides that they have already included in their total, to avoid counting sides more than once'.

Year 5 statutory: 'measure and calculate the perimeter of composite rectilinear shapes in centimetres and metres'. Y5 non-statutory: 'Pupils calculate the perimeter of rectangles and related composite shapes, including using the relations of perimeter or area to find unknown lengths.'
learnerActions: Trace a finger (or pen) all the way around the boundary of an L-shaped figure, naming or ticking each side as you pass it so no side is counted twice and none is missed.

When you reach an unmarked side, work out its length from the labelled sides: the two shorter sides along a direction add up to the opposite longer side, so find a missing longer side by adding the two shorters, or find a missing shorter side by subtracting the known shorter length from the longer. Write the deduced length on the blank.
Keep a running total as you go; when every side is ticked, read off the perimeter in cm.
Notice the internal 'fold' line where the rectangles join: leave it out — it is not part of the boundary.
activities.intendedInsight: A hidden side length is not missing information: it can be recovered from the labelled sides, because the shorter sides along a direction add up to the opposite longer side. Perimeter is the total distance around the boundary, each side counted exactly once, excluding internal lines.

activities.title: Find-the-missing-side, total, and spot-the-mistake
feedback: If you included a line inside the shape, remember perimeter is only the outer boundary — trace it to check.
If you gave a cm2 answer, you have found area, not perimeter; perimeter is a length in cm, the total of the sides.
For a missing side, point to the opposite side(s) of the whole shape: the total length across in that direction must balance.
activities.rationale: Compute-perimeter, find-missing-side and spot-the-mistake items probe the skill and its characteristic errors directly. A recognition (multiple-choice) spot-the-mistake item checks diagnosis but does not by itself require the pupil to construct a full perimeter from scratch, so pair it with an open compute task.
sourceClaims: A rectilinear/compound shape has only straight sides and right angles (rectangles joined). Things to look out for: 'children may miscount when adding the sides of rectilinear shapes'; 'if children do not have a secure understanding of addition and subtraction, they may struggle when finding missing sides'; 'children may find it difficult to see that the two shorter sides are equal to the longer opposite side'. A reasoning task shows a character whose total wrongly 'includes sides that are inside the shape'. Children are 'encouraged to mark sides that they have already included in their total, to avoid counting sides more than once'.
Learners commonly confuse area and perimeter, often because the concepts and their formulae are met together without conceptual grounding.
learnerActions: Given an L-shape with some sides labelled and some blank, find each unmarked side by adding or subtracting the labelled lengths along that direction, then total the whole perimeter.

Examine a worked solution where a character has made an error — e.g. included an internal join-line, or omitted an unmarked side — and say exactly which side is wrong and what the correct total should be.
Decompose the shape into rectangles to see why the two shorter sides add up to the opposite longer side.
activities.intendedInsight: The method has two stages — deduce all unknown sides, then add every boundary side once — and the common errors (adding only given numbers, including inside lines, double-counting, giving area instead) are specific and checkable.

activities.title: Draw a composite shape to a target perimeter
feedback: If your total isn't 40 cm, re-trace the boundary and re-add, ticking each side once.
Check your shape only has right angles and straight sides; a diagonal or curve changes the task.
Make sure the lengths across the shape in each direction agree with each other.
activities.rationale: Production (drawing and labelling to a constraint) elicits independent construction that a recognition item does not by itself require, and the draw-and-check task still exercises the curriculum skill of calculating the perimeter of a composite shape; it matches the stated evidence of drawing a composite shape with a given perimeter.
sourceClaims: Year 5 statutory: 'measure and calculate the perimeter of composite rectilinear shapes in centimetres and metres'. Y5 non-statutory: 'Pupils calculate the perimeter of rectangles and related composite shapes, including using the relations of perimeter or area to find unknown lengths.'
learnerActions: On cm paper, draw a composite rectilinear shape (rectangles joined, straight sides that always meet at right angles) whose perimeter is exactly 40 cm.
Label every side and check that the total length across the shape in each direction balances.
Add all the boundary sides to confirm the total is 40 cm, ticking each side once.
activities.intendedInsight: Constructing a shape to a given perimeter — not just reading one — requires the pupil to control which sides are boundary, how deduced sides relate, and to keep length (cm) distinct from area.

constraints: Define rectilinear/compound shape explicitly (only straight sides, with sides always meeting at right angles, including the inward corner of an L-shape; rectangles joined) and use both terms.

Include figures with unmarked sides so the deduction step is genuinely required; fully-labelled shapes given to read off only practise addition, not the distinctive skill (the draw-your-own task, where the pupil labels all sides they create, is a separate production activity).
Mark/tick each side as it is added to prevent missing or double-counting a side.
Distinguish the boundary (perimeter) from internal split/join lines, which are excluded.
Keep perimeter (length, cm) distinct from area (cm2); address the common area/perimeter confusion explicitly.
Secure addition and subtraction underpin missing-side deduction; reteach these prerequisites if the pupil cannot combine the known lengths.

Tap-to-reveal or lit-side animations are optional scaffolds that illustrate the method but do not by themselves give the pupil tracing or counting practice — follow them with pupil-constructed working.
A spot-the-mistake multiple-choice item checks error-diagnosis but does not require constructing a full perimeter; include at least one open compute or draw task.

State the relationship precisely: in each direction, the side lengths on one side of the shape SUM to the side lengths on the opposite side. In an L-shape, the two shorter sides along a direction SUM to the opposite longer side, and other composite shapes may have more than two parts on one side. Subtraction is only how a missing shorter side is recovered (longer minus a known shorter), not a restatement that the shorter sides 'equal' the longer.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy 'poor fit' claims that 3D 'adds nothing' and that the learning 'is not a dialogue' were removed as catalog-preference boilerplate; a 2D/paper representation suits planar shapes well, but no source establishes that other media could not also support aspects of the task.

Geometric idealisation note: a drawn or screen figure represents an idealised plane shape; cm-paper cutouts have real thickness and only approximate the ideal figure. This does not affect the perimeter arithmetic but is worth flagging if physical cutouts are used.

Diagnostic example in the source (outer 8 cm and 6 cm with a notch and two unmarked sides) was retained conceptually; exact numeric consistency of any specific L-shape used should be checked so that opposite directions genuinely balance before giving it to a learner.

The White Rose source phrases the relationship as the two shorter sides being 'equal to' the opposite longer side; the accurate statement is that they SUM to it. Learner-facing text uses 'add up to', and subtraction is described only as the operation for recovering a missing shorter side, not as a restatement of the relationship. The verbatim source wording is preserved only within sourceClaims.

Activity 3's DfE sourceClaim grounds the perimeter-calculation content the drawing task exercises; the production-over-recognition point is treated as a narrow objective affordance, not as source-proven efficacy.

probeDeeper: Which sides weren't labelled? How did you work out their lengths?
Trace the perimeter with your finger — did you include any line inside the shape?
How do you know you counted every side exactly once?
If I asked for the area instead, would you do the same thing?
assess.correctAnswer: Deduces the two unmarked sides from the labelled ones (opposite sides of the whole are equal, found by adding or subtracting known lengths), adds all boundary sides exactly once, and gives the perimeter in cm.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds only the labelled numbers and forgets to find the unmarked sides.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mark every side of the shape; deduce each unmarked side from the opposite labelled sides before adding anything.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sums the given lengths and stops, omitting the two unmarked sides.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mis-deduces a missing side — does not see that the two shorter sides equal the opposite longer side.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Line up the shape's opposite sides and add or subtract the known lengths to find the missing one; use the decomposition into rectangles to see the relationship.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Guesses or mislabels an unmarked side rather than adding/subtracting the known lengths.

errorPatterns.pattern: Includes an internal split-line, double-counts a side, or confuses perimeter with area.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace the boundary with a finger (perimeter is the distance around) and tick each side once; contrast cm (length) with cm² (area).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Adds a line inside the shape, counts a side twice, or multiplies to give an area instead.

responseLevels.gap: Adds only the given numbers, or includes internal lines / confuses with area; no missing-side reasoning.
responseLevels.full: Deduces unmarked sides from the labelled ones, adds every boundary side exactly once (excluding internal lines), and gives the perimeter in cm, keeping it distinct from area.
responseLevels.partial: Finds the perimeter when all sides are labelled but cannot reliably deduce unmarked sides, or occasionally double-counts; the method is present but not secure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child an L-shaped figure on cm paper with only some sides labelled (e.g. an outer 8 cm and 6 cm, and a notch with two sides given but two sides left unmarked). Say: 'Find its perimeter.' Then WATCH whether they deduce the unmarked sides from the labelled ones, whether they add every boundary side exactly once (and not the internal line), and whether they confuse it with area.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: An L-shape with unmarked sides forces the deduction step, so a child who only adds the visible numbers is exposed at once; whether they trace the boundary (excluding internal lines) and avoid double-counting is visible in the working, which is why the task is set and watched.
